name: Vietnamese (Northern)
sources: Kirby, James P. (2011). Vietnamese (Hanoi Vietnamese). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(3), 381-392.
Thompson, Laurence C. (1965). A Vietnamese Grammar. University of Washington Press.
Nguyễn, Văn Lợi & Edmondson, Jerold A. (1998). Tones and voice quality in modern northern Vietnamese: instrumental case studies. Mon-Khmer Studies 28, 1-18.
Michaud, Alexis (2004). Final consonants and glottalization: new perspectives from Hanoi Vietnamese. Phonetica 61, 119-146.
Pham, Andrea Hoa (2003). Vietnamese Tone: A New Analysis. Routledge.
Brunelle, Marc (2009). Tone perception in Northern and Southern Vietnamese. Journal of Phonetics 37, 79-96.
Brunelle, Marc (2009). Northern and Southern Vietnamese tone coarticulation: a comparative case study. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 1.
Han, Mieko S. & Kim, Kong-On (1974). Phonetic variation of Vietnamese tones in disyllabic utterances. Journal of Phonetics 2, 223-232.
Kirby, James (2010). Dialect experience in Vietnamese tone perception. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 127(6).

Đỗ, Thế Dũng, Trần, Thiên Hương & Boulakia, Georges (1998). Intonation in Vietnamese. In Daniel Hirst & Albert Di Cristo (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Brunelle, Marc, Hạ, Kiều Phương & Grice, Martine (2012). Intonation in Northern Vietnamese. The Linguistic Review 29(1), 3-36.
contrasts: six tones that differ in pitch contour and in voice quality
implosive ɓ ɗ against voiceless unaspirated t, k and aspirated tʰ; there is no aspirated labial or velar stop (f and x fill those places)
long against short in two vowel pairs, a against ă and ɤ against ɤ̆, in closed syllables only
back unrounded ɯ ɤ against back rounded u o
final stops p t k against final nasals m n ŋ
three centring diphthongs iə ɯə uə
allophony: ɓ and ɗ are fully voiced and usually implosive or preglottalised; they are the only voiced stops
t is dental and unaspirated, tʰ alveolar and aspirated
written ch and tr are the same sound in Hanoi, a palatal affricate [tɕ]; written s and x are both [s]; written d, gi and r are all [z]: there are no retroflex consonants
final p t k are unreleased
after the front vowels i e ɛ, final k and ŋ are fronted to pre-velar or palatal (written ch, nh) and the vowel is shortened, with a palatal offglide on a (anh, ách)
after the rounded vowels u o ɔ, final k and ŋ are doubly articulated labial-velars [k͡p̚], [ŋ͡m] and the vowel is shortened and diphthongised (học, ông)
ɣ is a voiced velar fricative, sometimes a stop; x is a voiceless velar fricative
a syllable written with an initial vowel begins with a glottal stop
in closed syllables a long vowel is followed by a shorter coda and a short vowel by a longer coda
syllable_structure: (C)(w)V(C) plus tone; the coda is one of p t k m n ŋ or a glide j, w
phonotactics: syllables ending in p t k carry only the sắc or the nặng tone
the short vowels ă and ɤ̆ occur only in closed syllables
medial w does not follow labial initials in native words
p is initial only in loanwords

stress.rule: The last syllable of a phrase is the most prominent; grammatical words and the first syllable of many compounds and reduplications are weaker.
stress.cues: duration, intensity and fuller realisation of the tone contour

length.notes: Length is contrastive only for a against ă and ɤ against ɤ̆, and only in closed syllables. No ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; mild declination and a lower, more fully realised final tone
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by particles (không, à, hả, chưa); the pitch register is raised overall and the last syllable is higher, without a fixed rising boundary tone
intonation.wh_question: question word in place; register somewhat raised; often a final particle
intonation.continuation: phrase-final lengthening and sustained pitch, then reset
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; emphasis widens the pitch range and lengthens the syllable
intonation.notes: Brunelle, Hạ & Grice (2012) find that Northern Vietnamese intonation is gradient and varies between speakers, with no set of categorical boundary tones; sentence-final particles do much of the work.

tone.confidence_notes: The contour shapes and voice qualities are well established; the Chao digits are the conventional ones and sources differ by one step (ngang 33 or 44, sắc 35 or 24, hỏi 313 or 312, nặng 21 or 32 with glottal stop).

inventory.name: ngang (A1), level; no tone mark
espeak_aliases: 7 (used on the last stressed syllable of a clause)
inventory.description: Mid level, slightly falling before a pause.

inventory.name: huyền (A2), low falling; grave accent
inventory.description: Starts low-mid and falls gently to the bottom of the range.
inventory.phonation: breathy or lax for many speakers

inventory.name: sắc (B1), rising; acute accent
inventory.description: Starts mid, stays level briefly, then rises to high. In syllables ending in p t k it is short and high rising (45).

inventory.name: hỏi (C1), low falling-rising; hook above
inventory.description: Falls from mid to low, then in citation form rises again toward mid.
inventory.connected_speech: 31: the final rise is usually missing except before a pause or under emphasis
inventory.phonation: modal to creaky; often laryngealised at the low point

inventory.name: ngã (C2), broken rising; tilde
inventory.description: Starts mid, is interrupted in the middle of the vowel by glottal constriction (creak or a full glottal stop), during which pitch drops or becomes irregular, then rises sharply to the top of the range, higher than the end of sắc. Usually written 3ˀ5.
inventory.connected_speech: same shape; the constriction may weaken to creak in fast speech
inventory.phonation: glottal constriction or creaky voice in the middle of the vowel

inventory.name: nặng (B2), low glottalised; dot below
inventory.description: Starts low-mid and falls quickly, cut off by glottal closure; usually written 21ˀ. In syllables ending in p t k it is a short low fall.
inventory.phonation: creaky, ending in a glottal stop

sandhi: gradient tonal coarticulation only: carry-over (progressive) assimilation is stronger than anticipatory effects (Han & Kim 1974; Brunelle 2009)
hỏi loses its final rise in non-final position
tone.notes: Nguyễn & Edmondson (1998) show with F0 tracks and laryngoscopy that Northern tones combine pitch with phonation: huyền is breathy, ngã has a glottal interruption followed by a steep high rise, nặng drops and ends in glottal closure, and hỏi varies between speakers. Brunelle (2009) shows that Northern listeners use voice quality as well as pitch to identify tones, above all for ngã and nặng. No absolute F0 values are given here.

phonation: breathy or lax voice on huyền
glottal constriction in the middle of ngã
creaky voice and final glottal closure on nặng
laryngealisation at the low point of hỏi for many speakers

problems: no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c ignores the clause type, and a question gives the same audio as a statement; the only clause-level change is that an unmarked (ngang) last syllable is given tone 7, a slightly higher level
voice quality is not modelled: huyền is not breathy, and the glottalisation of ngã and nặng is imitated only by a dip in amplitude (envelopes vi_5amp and vi_6amp) while voicing continues
nặng is not short: its length reduction is commented out in ph_vietnam, and mạ lasts as long as mả and mã (about 340 ms measured)
hỏi always has the full fall and rise, also inside a phrase, where the natural form is a low fall without the rise
ɓ is spoken with the plain voiced b of the base table, with a short pause before it at the start of a word, not as an implosive; ɗ has its own recording
no tonal coarticulation, and the voice attribute 'words 1 2' puts a pause between all words, so speech is staccato
sắc and nặng in stop-final syllables use the same pitch contours as in open syllables; only the vowel is shorter
good: six tones with distinct contours (level, low fall, rise, fall-rise, dip with high rise, fall), and the two glottalised tones are set apart by amplitude dips
the tonal range is wider than in eSpeak's other tone languages: about 95 to 147 Hz with the voice setting 'pitch 95 175' (about 7.5 semitones, measured)
vowel durations depend on the coda: short before final stops, longer before nasals, longest in open syllables
the Hanoi mergers are right: tr is ch, s is x, and d, gi, r are all z
dental unaspirated t, aspirated th, the velar fricatives and the short vowels ă, â are present, and rhymes with labial-velar finals (ong, ông, oc, ôc) have their own vowel phonemes

notes: eSpeak NG tone numbers: 1 ngang, 2 huyền, 3 sắc, 4 hỏi, 5 ngã, 6 nặng, 7 clause-final ngang. The voice file has no phonemes line, so the table is chosen by the language name.
